newsitem.title: USA: Ex-Daiwa trader gets 4 year prison term.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Daiwa trader gets 4 year prison term.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Law Correspondent
A former Daiwa Bank Ltd. bond trader was sentenced to four years in prison and fined $2 million Monday for conspiring to hide $1.1 billion in losses, among the biggest ever from unauthorised trades.
Toshihide Iguchi, 45, a Japanese-born bond trader who worked in Daiwa Bank's New York office, also was ordered to repay the bank $570,000 in restitution for the amount he had stolen from it.

U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan, who could have sentenced Iguchi to more than 10 years in prison, said he was giving a shorter sentence because of Iguchi's extraordinary cooperation and the suffering it has caused him. He has been branded in the Japanese press as a traitor for informing U.S. authorities about his employer's crimes.
"You are to segments of your country a pariah," Kaplan said.
Iguchi told the judge he had struggled with whether the "right thing to do" would be to remain loyal to Daiwa or cooperate with U.S. authorities in a move that could hurt his employer.
"After much soul-searching ... I came to the conclusion that the right thing to do regardless of the consequences is to tell the truth at all costs," Iguchi said.
"Over the years I've learned that it takes an enormous amount of strength and courage to live a life of total honesty," he said.
Although Kaplan gave Iguchi a reduced term, he denied a plea by Iguchi's lawyer that his client be sentenced to 18 months and receive credit for 15 months already served.
"There is no question that this was a crime of historical dimensions and potentially world shattering implications," Kaplan said.
He said he must send a message to those holding power who could threaten the world's banking systems that even the most extensive cooperation would not win them a "slap on the wrist."
Iguchi pleaded guilty in October 1995, when he told another federal judge that senior managers at the Japanese bank lied to the Federal Reserve about his activities.

As part of the agreement with prosecutors, Iguchi, who was senior executive vice president of the bank's New York branch, admitted six counts of misapplying bank funds, false entries in bank books and records, money laundering and conspiracy. He admitted incurring the trading losses over a 12-year period.

Iguchi's information led authorities to obtain an indictment against Daiwa and in February, the bank pleaded guilty to 16 charges that it covered up Iguchi's trading losses and agreed to pay a record $340 million fine, the largest ever for a financial institution.
Daiwa officials learned of Iguchi's activities when he sent the bank's president a 30-page confession on July 13, 1995. The bank did not inform U.S. officials for six weeks.
Although Daiwa pleaded guilty, it has not cooperated with U.S. authorities. Kaplan slammed Daiwa during the hearing for its attitude and said the bank had "manifested extraordinary culpability."
"Daiwa Bank has acted with exceptional contempt of U.S. law. It has refused to cooperate with U.S. authorities to this date," the judge said.
U.S. Attorney Mary Jo White said the Daiwa probe was continuing.

Kaplan said he would not order Iguchi to make full restitution to the bank for its losses, not only because the defendant will be penniless but because such a payment would more than offset the amount Daiwa had paid as a fine.

The losses were among the biggest ever from unauthorised trading. Japanese trading giant Sumitomo Corp. in June disclosed $1.8 billion in losses from unauthorised trades and fired former star copper trader Yasuo Hamanaka. Ex-Barings Plc trader Nick Leeson helped bring down the venerable British investment bank after racking up losses of $1.4 billion in February 1995.
Kaplan said he was convinced that Iguchi had not acted out of greed but compared him to an "uncontrollable" gambler who panics and continues to bet to try to cover his losses.
Kaplan said Iguchi desperately tried to recoup the losses with "one more roll of the dice.
"Unfortunately you were neither good at it or lucky," the judge said.
Masahiro Tsuda, former general manager of Daiwa's New York branch, also pleaded guilty to his role in the scandal and was sentenced in October to two months in prison and fined $100,000.
